It is recognized that war may come at any time and it behooves us in this house to think seriously about these things. We must override political differences in order to plan in such a way that real democracy will work. If the bickerings and foolishness go on I am sure that, while we are fighting, communism will come in through the back door. You are not going to stop it unless you can offer a better ideology than the communists offer.
This is not the time to fool; we should be as serious as possible. We should plan our economy so that we could underwrite job security. By job security I mean that there would be actually more jobs than we have workers. That is what I consider to be full employment. The dominion government

The Address-Mr. E. G. McCullough should take control of those industries which would be necessary to provide that full employment.
The government should take over those industries which manufacture armaments and which carry on preparations for war. I refer to the large steel corporations and other corporations that can make profits out of war or even out of the fear of war. Those corporations should be owned and controlled by the people. But that is not the picture that has developed since 1945. We in this group have fought against the policy of turning back to private industry those crown corporations which were built up with the money of the taxpayers. I need to name only a few.
There was the Consolidated Smelting plant at Calgary which cost the Canadian taxpayers $18 million and which was handed back for 25 cents on the dollar. There was the Research Enterprise building No. 14 which was turned back to the Corning Glass Company, a company which was indicted in the United States. Here we have the picture of the government once again permitting the entrenchment of big business and vested interests so that they can lead us down the path to another war.
The government has set up the Combines Investigation Act, now under the administration of Mr. McGregor, in order to stop the growth of monopoly in this country. It was recognized by every one that there was a danger from cartelization and monopolies in this country. I have here four publications arising from the work of Mr. McGregor and his associates. In 1945 he published a report entitled "Canada and International Cartels".
I want to read one or two of the recommendations of the commissioner. There are some ten recommendations in all. Mr. McGregor has this to say in paragraph No. 2 of his recommendations and conclusions:
Those examples illustrate the power of cartels to eliminate competition and to control production and distribution in wide areas of trade. The allocation of markets through restrictive arrangements made by private interested parties impinges on government authority over foreign trade and may nullify national trade policies developed to serve wider public interests. Government policies to encourage either imports or exports may prove ineffective if private barriers to such trade are erected by cartels. The reservation of the domestic market to particular producers may be as effective as a prohibitory tariff in barring imports. The allocation of import or export quotas by cartel agreement subjects foreign trade to quantitative limitation although such control may run counter to public policy. Ways must be found to prevent private business organized as cartels from supplanting government in the establishment of such commercial policies.
In paragraph No. 4 he has this to say:
The post-war period will require flexibility in industrial organization and operations, rather than 

restrictive arrangements designed to maintain the status quo. Industrial progress will be assisted by government policies directed to the elimination of restrictions on trade and by positive measures to promote expansion of trade and thus prevent the development of demoralized markets.
' Today our farmers are facing a decline in their markets. I have a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen of today in which Sir Stafford Cripps intimates that his government will have to cut down on the bacon and eggs imported from Canada. We find that in the United States also the agricultural market is slipping. I think it behooves us to plan for an international agreement, and to break cartelization in the industrial field so that we may have a free exchange of trade.
I advocate among other things, Mr. Speaker, that the government plan a national marketing act for our farmers, and secondly that they institute long-term agreements with other countries on the block trading barter basis if currency difficulties are in the way so that we may have the free flow of Canadian food products to the hungry countries abroad, and in exchange bring back the things which we need in Canada.
I think we have to do something for our veterans. We either have to roll back prices or we have to increase their allowances so that they can rehabilitate themselves. Of the 90,000 student veterans, about 42,000 have either finished university, or through financial difficulties have had to leave university. There are many black spots that have to be cleared away. I am very sorry that the government has failed to remove them, because if we go down we all go down together. Those of us in our little orbit of mankind must gird ourselves and be strong. In the words of the poet:
We are not here to play, to dream, to drift;
We have hard work to do and loads to lift.
Fear not the struggle, 'tis God's gift.
Be strong.

Mr. Speaker, as I was walking down to the chamber this evening an hon. member reminded me that I have spoken on hogs, I have also spoken on sheep, and in fact I have even mentioned turkeys. "But," he said to me, "why not mention horses?" It is a very simple matter for me to mention any kind of living thing because I have not spent my life with artificial things such as pens, pencils, paper and figures. I have been working during the past twenty-five or thirty years with germ cells, with chromosomes and determiners, with living things, with life itself. I have never worked for God, as some of these false preachers claim they are, but I have worked along with God. In fact, I have hobnobbed with Him for some time, figuratively speaking,

of course. I said to God one day: "Do you mind my taking your place for a while?" "No, no", He said, "go ahead; you will learn a few things." So I climbed upon a mound, the usual one outside the barn door, and when my feet began to get warm I said, "let there be life", and lo and behold there was life. I could say, "there shall be no life", and there was none; for I determined which animals should mate. I determined whether an animal should breed or whether it should not reproduce itself. I determined whether it should live, whether it should die, or whether it should be enslaved.
When a human being begins to take the place of God upon earth that human being has got to be God Himself. I shall illustrate what I mean. Unfortunately I have to get up early in the morning, and one morning I was waiting for the bus about six o'clock. Shortly after six o'clock, the early morning bus passes the street where I live. It is necessary that I come down here early in the morning because some short-sighted, long-legged, broad-bottomed, narrow-minded bureaucrat neglected to supply members of parliament, the representatives of the people, with sufficient office space. The early morning is the only time I can efficiently do my work undisturbed. We are crowded together in a small room, so crowded that if I lean back in my chair I strike the back of the chair occupied by the other member. It is the most disgraceful condition that exists in this parliament today. I have seen these bureaucrats, with their private secretaries, occupying sumptuous offices. Have I a private secretary? No, I have not. I have done all my own secretarial work, including typing, for the past two and a half years.
I was standing there waiting for the bus. Daylight was just dawning, and thinking of home, my sweetheart-who is my wife-and my children, I heard a slight rustling beside me. I looked down and it was an old tomcat wearily wending his way home. It stopped as it got halfway across the sidewalk, looked up at me, and I will swear it winked at me. It then crossed the road very slowly and disappeared among the garbage cans on its way home, where it would be mauled by the kids. Two slaves were the next form of life that came along. I looked at the face of the first one and found it entirely lacking in expression. I looked at the face of the second one and found it had no expression either. The first was pulling a wagon; the second was on the seat, holding the reins and driving the first. As I said before, I have dealt with life, with living things, and I recognize expressions on animal faces that would not be recognized by those not accustomed to looking for them. If one wants to know what sort of master a
The Address-Mr. Ashby slave has, look at the faces of the animals under his control. I have made these tests, and I would like hon. members to make similar tests in any town or city of any Christian country on the face of this earth. You will find that the expression on the faces of young people is hopeful. When they reach the age of eighteen or twenty that expression of hope begins to disappear, and by the time they are forty or forty-five you will not find more than one out of every fifteen people on the streets who smile. The reason is that Christians are being enslaved today.
Unfortunately my time is going very rapidly; if someone would only plug the hands of that clock I would be able to deal with these matters more fully, because they are very important. There is such a thing as what I call natural wisdom. Let me put it this way. The result of God's work is perfection. Did God make living things without endowing them with wisdom? Of course not. When we look at horses we think they are dumb brutes. I remember my neighbour, a poor elderly woman, coming to our house with both eyes blackened, her nose broken and her teeth knocked out. I did not ask what her husband had done to her because I knew he had died some time before and that could not be his fault; but I asked, what in the world had happened to her. She told me that she was looking out the kitchen window while washing the dishes, and saw poor old Nellie, the old mare, standing by the well waiting for a drink. So she dried her hands on her apron and ran out to give the horse a drink of water. No sooner did she get near the animal than it turned and kicked her squarely in the face. Many people would say that horse was vicious, but the fact is that the horse was not to blame because the natural wisdom with which it had been endowed originally had been distorted and rendered dormant, shall we say, by restricting its freedom. It was a slave. When you have an animal like that the only solution is to give it freedom. Crime is a result of slavery.
Now let me give you an illustration of what I mean by natural wisdom. If any hon. member of this house would volunteer for an experiment I will guarantee he would not be able to equal the humble horse when it comes to natural wisdom, for the human mind has been distorted. Take any volunteer, blindfold him and take him a given distance away, in a direction and to an area of which he has no knowledge whatever. He does not know where he is going, nor how far. Then take the blindfold off, if you like; put him in a box car; close the doors; transport him in any direction, north, south, east or west, for a given length of time. He does not know how long he has been traveling, nor at what
898

The Address-Mr. Ashby speed nor in what direction. Take him out of the box car and in another direction for a predetermined distance. Then after a couple of years, without contact with other human beings who might give him instructions, tell him to walk directly to the point from which he started. I do not think a human being alive today could possibly do that; yet I can show you horses that have done it, some of them travelling a distance of up to sixty-five miles, covering an area over which they had never traveled before. That is what I call natural wisdom.
Our troubles today, Mr. Speaker, are due to the fact that the natural wisdom with which we were endowed by God is being interfered with by human beings who deal in false ideas. When our children go to school, to college and university, if they remain there long enough they will be rendered incapable of thinking correctly and sanely. What we call universities are really nothing but elaborate barber schools or training factories, where our youths no longer receive an education but are trained for various professions, and the false and artificial instruction they receive renders the individual incapable of thinking naturally and sanely. Let me give you an illustration of what I mean. I have in my hand a copy of Industry, the official organ of the Canadian Manufacturers Association. I think I know the man who has been writing these articles; I believe I have been in touch with him, and if he keeps it up, one of these days I am going to name that individual because the day is rapidly approaching when we shall have to identify ourselves, just as we do in this parliament. When a vote is called and the bell rings we stand and identify ourselves for or against whatever it may be. I shall have to read this. It is only three or four short paragraphs, and I will hurry through it. The title is, "Money on Trees" and it reads:
Windfalls do occur. As a matter of fact, it's not so long ago that a gentleman in an Ontario industrial centre received the pleasant news that he had won the tidy sum of $34,000 simply because he held a sweepstakes ticket on the winner of the Manchester handicap.
All that happened there, of course, was that one man gained what other men lost.
But the best brains of this and any age still persist that there is no substitute for hard work-
I guarantee that this man has avoided hard work. If he believed in it he would be working on a farm or in a mine or factory; he would be doing hard work. The fact is that he has learned a way of avoiding hard work. -in the task of getting on in the world, while practically every father has at some time or another come up with the none too original pronouncement to his children that money doesn't grow on trees.
fMr. Ashby.]
Unfortunately, there is more than a fair share of the globe's population suffering from the delusion that money does grow on trees.
I want all members to pay particular attention to this part because it is very important.
Witness the state of Oregon, which held an autumn referendum on a scheme to pay a pension of $50 a month to all men of 65 and over and the same amount to all women of 60 and over, even without the "means" test. The Oregonians not only approved the plan with a whacking majority, but on the same ballot plumped for higher income tax exemptions.
The people of Oregon were perfectly right. If the people of Oregon would discharge from office every individual who opposes this demand, I would give these individuals thirty days to do it and, if they did not, I would kick out the whole lot of them. It is possible to give this money to the people, as I will show you within the next few minutes.
This man says further:
Came the dawn and a study of practical details.
This man is deliberately lying when he talks about the practical details, for these are impractical, artificial details. This man's mind is polluted, as I will show you before I am through.
Somebody with a flair for mathematics-
That makes me think that if we could take these bureaucrats with a flair for mathematics and place them in an institution where they would be provided with an abundance of paper and pencils, as well as boys who would sharpen pencils for them, they could do all their estimating and planning there. When these plans and estimates were finished, they could be rushed into the next room where another group could tear them apart. This process could be continued until they all died and the world would be far better off. We do not need them.
Somebody with a flair for mathematics discovered to his and the state government's horror, that in 1949 there would be more than 175,000 male and female Oregonians eligible for the pension and that the cost to the state would be in excess of $100 million a year.
That also is a lie because it would not cost the state of Oregon one dollar. Think of that for just a moment. I know there is laughter, but I hope before the hon. members who are here die they will recognize the truth of that statement. The greatest mind in the world today is that possessed by a man now living whose name is Major C. H. Douglas. This man has given us a law which I shall quote to you so it will be on the record. "The true cost of production is the consumption of all production over a given period of time." This law should be written in capital letters and people should read it until they memorize it.
I remember standing in this house some two or three years ago, when I said the cost

of this chair was the chair. I am hesitating so my words will be fully appreciated. The price may have been $50 or $100, but the cost is this chair. True, it is not all of the cost, but most of the cost. The cost of production is what is consumed, as well as what is lost, of course, in the form of sawdust. Instead of a tree we have the chair. We still have the chair; it has not been consumed. If we burn the chair, then it is consumed and we have exchanged being able to sit down in the chair for the heat obtained from it. The cost of production is what is consumed.
If you go outside of this building and ask anyone you meet what he thinks this building cost, you will be told it must have cost hundreds of millions of dollars. What is a dollar? I asked this question last year and I received some of the most stupid, imbecile answers it is possible for the human mind to conceive. I received these answers from the official bureaucrats who are employed with the money of which we are robbing the people. I will read one of these answers to you. I asked these questions: Who owns this paper money? Who owns this metal money? Who owns the true dollars created by the banks? In my hand I hold the official answer I received to those questions, and I will read it to you:
This money is owned by the particular individuals, firms and corporations which have it in their possession.
Oh, rubbish! Let us see if this is true. Last year I copied from the Ottawa Journal of December 18, I think it was, something one of the magistrates had to say. Many of these magistrates and judges are almost as imbecile as these stupid bureaucrats. I am going to begin to mention names. This man is named Strike. Had I been there, I would have said, "Strike, you're out". Yes, sir, he missed the ball. According to the newspaper, this is what he said when sentencing some men:
One finds it a little difficult to understand how men like the two accused would commit such an offence.
These men were trying to avoid paying income taxes. Perhaps I had better read this article first and leave my remarks until later. The more one studies the works of Major Douglas, the more easily one can pick up any statement made by any Christian and find that his mind has been distorted; he cannot reason properly. In fact, I have found it difficult to do so myself. It is a tremendous relief for me to be able to recognize at least some truths today. Some years ago, I was just as dumb as anyone, for I also came under the influence of these false teachers.
The Address-Mr. Ashby
Magistrate Strike goes on to say:
It would appear that you have a good reputation in the community, that you were good employers and that you were considered to be reasonably good citizens.
My thought at that point is, why not leave them alone then? I shall continue to read the statement.
It is difficult to understand how you would stoop to commit such an offence as this. If it had not been for this tax investigation, you and your company would have had in your possession (money) the property of the treasury of Canada.
Let me illustrate, in this way, what the magistrate said. I am on my farm and someone comes to ask me for a dozen eggs. I say: "Those eggs do not belong to me, they belong to the hen-house", or the sheep belong to the sheep-shed or the cattle belong to the barn; all of this belongs to the farm, not to me. No one but an individual can own anything. These buildings own nothing. The only way that anything can possibly be owned is by individuals. In this case those in control of the treasury department are the ones that own the money. In other words, this man was a slave.
What is a slave? A slave is a person who has no property of his own and who is forced to toil for those who are his masters. What then is a free man? A free man is one who owns property which no man may take from him without his full will and consent. What right have these tax collectors to enter any home in this country or to take one single cent from any individual? They have no right, and they could never do it except by deceit and fraud. Instead of going as individuals and holding a revolver at the heads of citizens and demanding their money, they wave an order in council sneaked around parliament and say: this is the law; you are forced to hand over your hard-earned money.
Let me tell hon. members this. Merely because an individual is paid by the officials of a department to rob and plunder, and to commit these crimes, is no excuse, and will be no excuse in the hereafter. May I point out that each individual will, and should be, held responsible for his own actions. Yet these bureaucrats will tell you that it is the institution that is to blame, that it is the farm that is to blame, that it is the barns that are to blame. It is this, that and the other thing that is to blame; it is never "we are to blame." There is a key that will unlock the doors to freedom, security and peace on this earth, and this key we might call individual or personal responsibility, where each individual is held responsible for his own actions, which he cannot shirk and place upon any institution.

The Address-Mr. Ashby
I have read about half of the quotation.
I must get back to this Money on Trees-I forgot all about it-and finish this last paragraph. I had reached the point where these figure experts estimated that the cost would be $100 million a year. This man continues:
This astronomical figure turned out to be three times the state's budget for all purposes. Not only had the get-rich-quick voters ignored the fact that such a sum could not materialize except through ruinous taxes,-
Which is another lie, for taxes are not the only method of obtaining revenue.
-but they have voted for a tax reduction. All in all, the Oregon legislature is in a pretty fair pickle.
That is what he says. I would straighten him out. Let them hire me and give me the authority, and I will see that the Oregonians get their $50 a month. In fact, if the members of this house want our people to live decently, let them put me in charge and give me the authority. That is all I need. I will guarantee that every human being in Canada sixty years of age and over will obtain $50 a month, and I will do it without taxation. In fact, I will gradually abolish taxation altogether for revenue purposes as I will show before I am through.
I want to point out that the writer of this article was trained by these institutions of training to think in terms of what we call money economics-which is an unreal, artificial economics-instead of real, physical economics. This man does not estimate the amount of food, clothing or other essential needs of the people and then determine if we can supply these requirements.

It is all right to laugh. But I know from experience. I cannot help saying this, because I have such a wonderful wife myself. It does not matter what happens to your children, we men always say to them: you had better go to mother; mother knows best. I mention that for this reason. There perhaps lies the solution to the future problems of this country. But I must hustle along. I am constantly watching that clock. I think I shall have to let this go. It will take too much time. I will just quote rapidly:
The teaching of economics-
What kind of economics? Those unreal, artificial economics or real economics?
-and related subjects in American schools-
And Canadian schools are included.
-and especially in colleges and universities-has a profound influence on the economic life of the nation.
That is true. Our manufacturers are therefore trying to get young men who intend to study economics to work in a factory, to start at the bottom and grow up in it and use real things in order to obtain a contact with realities instead of specializing in all this artificial stuff.
Now I should like to illustrate hurriedly the work of some of these bureaucrats, the uselessness and stupidity of some of these poor imbeciles, because I cannot think of any other name to call them. Hon. members know that in the fall of the year for generations it has been customary for the farmer to butcher a hog or two for himself. A few days before he is ready to butcher the hog, he will gather up his equipment, consisting of a barrel or tank to hold the hot water, his implement to scrape the hair off the hog, basins, pails and all the rest of it. But when they go to get the knives from the kitchen the wife will say sometimes, "I wish you would use something else instead of my good knives". Therefore private enterprise, free enterprise as we call it, provides for everything. It does not matter what it may be. Take traveling equipment, for instance. I bought some beautiful bags for my wife-I mean traveling bags. They were really sturdy suitcases which were made by Cecil Sprigings and Company Limited. The price of these suitcases was between $60 and $70.
I discovered that if this firm were free of all these taxes imposed on them and these controls were removed, they could put these suitcases on the market actually better than they are-I could not see how they could

become any better-for half that price, or somewhere around $28. Individuals engaged in private enterprise say, "We will provide you with tools for every purpose, even to scrape the hair off the hogs. They manufacture a cheap little instrument. It has merely a wooden handle and a small metal disc on it; that is all. The price is only a few cents. Free enterprise, being what it is, plans months ahead. In July this particular storekeeper sent away and ordered five or six dozen cheap hog scrapers in order to accommodate his customers. I called at the store because one of my boys said, "When you are in town, dad, get a hog scraper; ours is lost. We want to butcher a hog". So I called in at the store and the gentleman came to me immediately and politely asked me what he could do for me. He asked me if he could serve me. I said: "I would like a hog scraper". Anyone would have thought that I had hit him square in the face. "Hog scraper!" he yelled at me, and he turned red in the face. "Don't talk to me about hog scrapers". I said: "I am Pat Ashby, a highfalutin' member of parliament; don't shout at me like that". He said: "You, a member of parliament, allowing these bureaucrats to carry on in this way. Look at this", he said, and he thrust into my hand a whole bundle of papers-and I hold them in my hand now. He ordered those hog scrapers in July but on August 25 he received a letter from these bureaucrats. He had written to them decently, for he said: "Dear Sir", and signed his name: "Yours truly", and so on. But these bureaucrats, these dictatorial scoundrels! I would soon put them all where they belong. If the people of Canada receive from any government department officials letters of any kind not signed "your obedient servant", they should return the letters without postage to the place from which they came. If enough people will do that these officials will learn who is the authority here in Canada and they will sign these letters as they should. What did this man say? He said: "Gentlemen!"
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will give me a few more minutes because I have had to

goes on:
This will acknowledge your application dated August 17 to import the following equipment.
The man lists them under three columns as follows: one, "supplier, Edmonton Butchers' and Packers' Supplies." That is a wholesale and retail store on Jasper avenue, Edmonton. But why tell him that? He knows that because he sent for them. In the second column appears the following:	"six dozen hog
scrapers"-the store keeper knew what he ordered-and under column three, "end users", those who scrape the hair off hogs. Can you imagine that? The letter continues:
It is noted that the end users are stated to be butchers . . . No letter of essentiality from the end users has been furnished, as required as per instructions on the reverse side of the application under paragraph three.
